Church History is the study of how Christianity's institutional structures, doctrines, and practices evolved across two thousand years. From small persecuted communities to the medieval Catholic establishment, then splintering through the Protestant Reformation, the Church has shaped politics, art, science, and culture across the Western world.

The early Church faced Roman persecution, including martyrdoms, until Constantine legalized Christianity in the fourth century. The Council of Nicaea in 325 CE then standardized doctrine. The rise of the papacy and the Eastern Orthodox schism in 1054 divided Christian leadership geographically and theologically, with the Pope claiming supremacy in the West while the Orthodox Patriarch was one voice among many. Medieval monasteries preserved learning, developed the Gregorian calendar, and served as centers of manuscript copying, education, and theological innovation during Europe's Dark Ages.

Thomas Aquinas and medieval scholasticism married Aristotelian philosophy with Christian theology, creating an intellectual synthesis that dominated European universities. The Protestant Reformation in the sixteenth century fractured Western Christianity into competing confessions including Lutheran, Reformed, Anglican, and Catholic traditions. Martin Luther's challenge to papal authority unleashed centuries of religious conflict. The Catholic Counter-Reformation responded with internal reforms through the Council of Trent, renewed missionary zeal through the Jesuits, and the Spanish Inquisition as an enforcement mechanism.

Church authority clashed with rising state power during the Enlightenment, reshaping the relationship between religion and governance as Enlightenment thinkers questioned clerical privilege and scriptural authority. Industrial-era secularization and the rise of biblical criticism through source analysis and the historical-critical method challenged traditional Church authority and sparked modernist versus fundamentalist debates that persist today.
